title: Zakah & Hajj
content_html:
Zakah — Almsgiving

Zakah is the third pillar of Islam and means “purification” or “growth.” By giving away a portion of their wealth, Muslims purify what remains and acknowledge that all wealth ultimately belongs to Allah. It is not considered charity in the voluntary sense — it is a compulsory duty for every Muslim whose savings exceed a minimum threshold called the nisab.

Key Fact

Muslims must give 2.5% of their annual savings above the nisab threshold. The Qur’an specifies eight categories of people who may receive Zakah, including the poor, the needy, those in debt, and travellers in difficulty (Qur’an 9:60).

Origins and Purpose

Zakah has its origins in the Qur’an and the practice of the Prophet Muhammad. The Qur’an links prayer and charity repeatedly: “Establish prayer and pay Zakah” (Qur’an 2:43). This shows that worship of God and care for others are inseparable in Islam. The purpose of Zakah is threefold: it purifies the giver from greed and selfishness, it supports those in genuine need, and it reduces inequality within the ummah.

For the giver: Zakah purifies wealth by removing attachment to material possessions. It reminds Muslims that everything they own is a trust from Allah and develops generosity and compassion. Muslims believe that giving Zakah brings spiritual reward and protects them on the Day of Judgement.

For the recipient: Zakah provides essential support for the poor, the sick, travellers in need and those in debt. It helps prevent extreme poverty and ensures basic needs are met. The Qur’an identifies eight specific categories of recipient (9:60), ensuring money reaches those who need it most.

For the community: Zakah reduces the gap between rich and poor, creating a more just and equal society. It strengthens social bonds within the ummah because the wealthy are directly responsible for supporting the vulnerable. In some Muslim-majority countries, Zakah is collected and distributed by the state.

Khums means “one fifth” and is an additional financial duty unique to Shi’a Islam. Shi’a Muslims pay 20% of their surplus income (after living expenses) each year. Half of the Khums goes to Sayyids (descendants of the Prophet) and half to religious scholars and institutions. Khums is one of the Ten Obligatory Acts and reflects the Shi’a emphasis on supporting the Prophet’s family and the religious leadership.

Key Fact

Zakah (2.5% of savings) is paid by all Muslims, while Khums (20% of surplus income) is an additional duty for Shi’a Muslims. Both serve the purpose of social justice and redistributing wealth, but Khums also supports the Prophet’s descendants and Shi’a religious institutions.

Hajj — Pilgrimage to Makkah

Hajj is the fifth pillar of Islam. Every Muslim who is physically and financially able must make the pilgrimage to Makkah at least once in their lifetime. Hajj takes place during the Islamic month of Dhul Hijjah and attracts over two million Muslims from around the world each year. The Qur’an states: “Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by people who are able to undertake it” (Qur’an 3:97).

Origins

Hajj traces its origins to the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham). Muslims believe that Ibrahim and his son Isma’il built the Ka’aba as the first house of worship dedicated to the one true God. Many of the rituals performed during Hajj commemorate events from Ibrahim’s life — his willingness to sacrifice his son, his wife Hajar’s search for water, and his rejection of Satan’s temptations.

How Hajj is Performed

Hajj lasts five to six days and involves a series of rituals at sacred sites in and around Makkah. Before beginning, pilgrims enter a state of ihram — they wear simple white garments (two unstitched cloths for men), symbolising equality before God. All distinctions of wealth, status and nationality are stripped away.

Tawaf: Pilgrims walk around the Ka’aba seven times in an anti-clockwise direction. This represents the unity of Muslims in worshipping one God. The Ka’aba is believed to be directly below God’s throne in heaven.

Sa’i: Pilgrims walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, re-enacting Hajar’s desperate search for water for her son Isma’il. This commemorates God’s provision of the Zamzam well.

Arafat: Pilgrims travel to the plain of Arafat and stand in prayer and reflection from noon to sunset. This is considered the most important ritual of Hajj — the Prophet Muhammad said: “Hajj is Arafat.” It represents standing before God on the Day of Judgement.

Muzdalifah: After sunset at Arafat, pilgrims travel to Muzdalifah where they pray, rest under the open sky, and collect pebbles for the next day’s ritual.

Mina — Stoning the Pillars: At Mina, pilgrims throw pebbles at three stone pillars representing the places where Ibrahim rejected Satan’s temptations. This symbolises the Muslim’s rejection of evil and temptation in their own life.

Sacrifice: An animal (usually a sheep or goat) is sacrificed at Mina, commemorating Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to God. The meat is distributed to the poor. This coincides with the festival of Id-ul-Adha celebrated by Muslims worldwide.

Key Fact

The key stages of Hajj include Tawaf (circling the Ka’aba), Sa’i (walking between Safa and Marwa), standing at Arafat, collecting pebbles at Muzdalifah, stoning the pillars at Mina, and animal sacrifice. Each ritual commemorates events from the life of Ibrahim and symbolises key aspects of Muslim faith.

title: Core Beliefs: Six Articles & Five Roots
content_html:
Why Core Beliefs Matter

Islam is built on a set of core beliefs that shape every aspect of a Muslim’s life — from daily worship to moral decision-making. These beliefs are not identical across all Muslims. The two main branches of Islam, Sunni and Shi’a, share many fundamental ideas but organise and emphasise them differently. Understanding both frameworks is essential For the exam .

The split between Sunni and Shi’a originated after the Prophet Muhammad’s death in 632 CE. Most Muslims chose Abu Bakr as Caliph (successor), forming the Sunni tradition. A minority believed Muhammad had appointed his cousin and son-in-law Ali as the rightful leader, forming the Shi’a tradition. This disagreement over leadership led to different ways of expressing shared beliefs.

The Six Articles of Faith (Sunni Islam)

Sunni Muslims summarise their core beliefs in the Six Articles of Faith, collectively known as Iman. These six beliefs come from the Qur’an and the Sunnah (the Prophet’s teachings and example). Believing in all six is considered essential for a Sunni Muslim.

1. Tawhid — Oneness of Allah. There is only one God. Allah is eternal, absolute and has no partners or children. The sin of Shirk (associating anything with Allah) is the only unforgivable sin. Surah 112 declares: “He is Allah, the One.”

2. Malaikah — Angels. Allah created angels from divine light. They have no free will and carry out His commands perfectly. They deliver revelations to prophets and record every person’s deeds for the Day of Judgement.

3. Kutub — Holy Books. Allah revealed guidance through several scriptures, including the Torah, Psalms, Gospel, Scrolls of Abraham and the Qur’an. Only the Qur’an is believed to remain uncorrupted — it is the direct, unchanged word of Allah.

4. Risalah — Prophethood. Allah chose prophets to deliver His message. Muhammad is the “Seal of the Prophets” — the final messenger. Surah 33:40 confirms this.

5. Akhirah — Day of Judgement and Afterlife. This life is a preparation for the next. Every person will be judged by Allah on the Day of Judgement. The righteous enter paradise (Jannah); the wicked face punishment in hell (Jahannam).

6. Al-Qadr — Predestination. Allah knows everything that has happened and will happen. Nothing occurs by chance. Surah 9:51 states: “Only what God has decreed will happen to us.”

Key Fact

The Six Articles of Faith are: (1) Tawhid, (2) Malaikah (angels), (3) Kutub (holy books), (4) Risalah (prophethood), (5) Akhirah (afterlife), and (6) Al-Qadr (predestination). Every Sunni Muslim must accept all six.

The Five Roots of Usul ad-Din (Shi’a Islam)

Usul ad-Din means “foundations of the faith.” These five principles guide Shi’a belief, and from them flow the Ten Obligatory Acts that shape Shi’a practice.

1. Tawhid — Oneness of Allah. Identical to the Sunni belief. Allah is one, unique and beyond comparison.

2. Adalat — Divine Justice. Allah is perfectly just and never acts unfairly. Surah 16:90 states: “Indeed Allah commands you towards justice.” Humans are accountable for their actions because Allah is fair in His judgement. This root is unique to Shi’a belief frameworks.

3. Nubuwwah — Prophethood. Allah sent prophets to guide humanity. Muhammad was the final prophet. This overlaps with the Sunni article of Risalah.

4. Imamate — Divinely Appointed Leadership. After Muhammad, twelve Imams from his family were chosen by Allah to lead the Muslim community. They are considered infallible. The twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, is believed to be in hiding and will return at the end of time. This belief has no equivalent in Sunni Islam.

5. Al-Ma’ad — Resurrection. On the Day of Judgement every person will be physically resurrected and judged by Allah on their deeds.

Key Fact

The Five Roots of Usul ad-Din are: (1) Tawhid, (2) Adalat (justice), (3) Nubuwwah (prophethood), (4) Imamate (leadership), and (5) Al-Ma’ad (resurrection). The key differences from Sunni articles are the inclusion of Adalat and the Imamate.

Similarities and Differences

Both traditions share fundamental beliefs: the oneness of Allah (Tawhid), the authority of the Qur’an, the prophethood of Muhammad, and accountability on the Day of Judgement. They also share the Five Pillars of Islam — the five practices that maintain the Muslim community.

Leadership: Sunni Muslims accepted four Rightly Guided Caliphs. Shi’a Muslims believe only Ali and the twelve Imams had divine authority to lead.

Belief frameworks: Sunni Muslims follow six articles; Shi’a Muslims follow five roots. Shi’a belief uniquely includes Adalat (divine justice) and the Imamate. Sunni belief separately lists angels, holy books and predestination as individual articles.

Sources of authority: Sunni Muslims rely on the Qur’an, Sunnah and scholarly consensus. Shi’a Muslims also follow the teachings of the infallible Imams.

For the exam, you need to explain both frameworks clearly and identify what is shared and what is distinct. Remember that these differences stem from the original dispute over leadership — both groups worship the same God and follow the same Qur’an.

title: Festivals and Commemorations
content_html:
Festivals and Commemorations in Islam

Muslims celebrate several important festivals throughout the year. You need to know three: Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, and Ashura. Each festival has distinct origins, and Muslims celebrate them in different ways depending on their denomination.

Eid al-Fitr — The Festival of Breaking the Fast

Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan, the holy month of fasting. The word “Eid” means “festival” and “Fitr” means “breaking the fast.” It is a joyful celebration that thanks Allah for the strength to complete the fast and for the revelation of the Qur’an, which took place during Ramadan.

Key Fact

The Qur’an states: “He wants that you must complete the same number of days, and that you must magnify Allah for having guided you so that you may be grateful to Him” (2:185). This verse connects the completion of Ramadan fasting directly to the celebration of Eid al-Fitr.

Preparations begin before the day itself. Muslims send cards, decorate their homes, buy new clothes, and prepare special food and gifts. On the morning of Eid, Muslims rise early, bathe, and eat something sweet — traditionally dates — before attending the Eid prayer. The Prophet Muhammad himself consumed dates before the Eid prayer, and Muslims follow this Sunnah.

Before the Eid prayer, Muslims give Zakat al-Fitr — a small charitable donation (approximately £2–£5) so that poorer Muslims can also celebrate. The Eid prayer takes place at the mosque or in an open area such as a park. After the prayer, the Imam delivers a sermon. Muslims then exchange gifts, visit friends and family, and share a special meal together. It is also Sunnah to take a different route home from the one taken to the prayer. Many Muslims visit the cemetery to remember loved ones and forgive friends or relatives they have fallen out with.

In Muslim-majority countries, Eid al-Fitr is a public holiday. In the UK, British Muslims are often allowed a day off school or work. The festival reinforces the sense of ummah (community) as Muslims come together to celebrate after a month of shared spiritual discipline.

Eid al-Adha — The Festival of Sacrifice

Eid al-Adha takes place during the month of Dhul Hijjah and coincides with the annual Hajj pilgrimage. It commemorates the Prophet Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son when commanded by Allah. According to Islamic tradition, Ibrahim told his son of Allah’s command, and his son replied that they must do as Allah demanded. However, at the moment of sacrifice, Allah provided a ram to be killed instead. This demonstrated Ibrahim’s complete submission to the will of Allah.

Key Fact

The Qur’an teaches that Ibrahim agreed to sacrifice his son even though he was tempted by Shaytan (the devil). At three places, the angel Jibril told Ibrahim to “Pelt him,” so Ibrahim threw seven pebbles and Shaytan left. This event is re-enacted during Hajj at the Jamarat stone pillars.

The central act of Eid al-Adha is the Qurbani — the sacrifice of an animal, usually a sheep or goat. The meat is divided into three portions: one third for the family, one third for friends and neighbours, and one third distributed to the poor. This ensures that everyone, regardless of wealth, can share in the celebration.

Muslims also attend special Eid prayers at the mosque, listen to a sermon, wear their best clothes, and exchange gifts. For pilgrims on Hajj, this is a particularly solemn moment — men shave their heads and women cut a lock of hair, symbolising the end of the main pilgrimage rituals. The festival lasts for up to three days.

Ashura — A Day of Remembrance

Ashura falls on the 10th day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar. It is significant for both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims, but its origins and the way it is commemorated differ greatly between the two denominations. This makes Ashura one of the clearest examples of Sunni–Shi’a differences in practice.

Key Fact

For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura commemorates the martyrdom of Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. For Sunni Muslims, it recalls the day Allah saved Musa (Moses) and the Israelites from slavery in Egypt by parting the Red Sea.

After the death of the Prophet Muhammad, a dispute arose over who should lead the Muslim community. Shi’a Muslims believed leadership should stay within the Prophet’s family. In 680 CE, Yazid succeeded his father Muawiyah as Caliph. Yazid demanded that Husayn, Muhammad’s grandson and son of Imam Ali, pledge allegiance to him. Husayn refused because he believed Yazid was religiously misguided and that the agreement for leadership to remain within the Prophet’s family had been broken.

The people of Kufa invited Husayn to join them in opposition to Yazid. On his way to Kufa, Yazid’s army forced Husayn, his family, and a small group of supporters to stop at Karbala. They were denied water and food. After about seven days, Husayn and most of his family and companions were killed in battle. Husayn was beheaded. Shi’a Muslims regard Husayn and his followers as martyrs who chose death rather than compromise their beliefs.

Shi’a Muslims treat Ashura as an intense day of mourning and sorrow. Many wear black mourning clothes, participate in processions to mark the martyrdom, and listen to accounts and poems about Husayn’s death, which may lead to weeping. Some Shi’a Muslims make pilgrimage to Husayn’s shrine in Karbala (called Mashad al-Husayn). Some practise self-flagellation or give blood to remember the blood shed by the martyrs. Others pray and visit the mosque, reflecting on how a true Muslim should be steadfast in their faith as Husayn was.

Sunni Muslims commemorate Ashura primarily through voluntary fasting, following the example of the Prophet Muhammad, who fasted when he learned that the Jews of Medina fasted on this day to remember Allah saving Musa from the Egyptians. Sunni Muslims may also help the less fortunate, repent their sins, ask for forgiveness, and pray at the mosque. In Turkey, some eat a special pudding called Nuh’s pudding.

Ashura is sometimes debated as a term. Some argue it should not be called a “festival” or “celebration” at all, particularly for Shi’a Muslims, because the mood is one of grief and mourning rather than joy. This contrasts sharply with the celebratory atmosphere of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha. Nevertheless, it remains one of the most significant dates in the Islamic calendar.

title: Al-Qadr, Akhirah & the Day of Judgement
content_html:
Al-Qadr — Predestination

Al-Qadr is the sixth article of Sunni faith. It means predestination — the belief that Allah already knows and has determined everything that will happen. Nothing occurs by accident or chance. Surah 9:51 states: “Only what God has decreed will happen to us. He is our Master.” This includes every event in a person’s life, from birth to death.

Muslims believe Allah has complete knowledge of the past, present and future. Before a child is born, an angel records four things about their life: their provision (livelihood), their lifespan, their deeds, and whether they will be happy or unhappy. This is written in the “Preserved Tablet” (Lawh al-Mahfuz), which contains the record of all that has been and all that will be.

Key Fact

Al-Qadr does not mean humans are puppets. Muslims believe Allah knows in advance what choices a person will make, but the person still makes those choices freely. It is this freedom that makes humans accountable on the Day of Judgement.

Predestination and Human Freedom

One of the most complex issues in Islamic theology is how predestination relates to human freedom. If Allah has already decided everything, can humans truly be free? And if they are not free, how can they be held responsible for their actions on the Day of Judgement?

Most Muslims hold that both beliefs are true simultaneously. Allah’s knowledge is absolute — He knows what every person will do before they do it. But this foreknowledge does not force people to act in a particular way. Humans have genuine freedom of choice (ikhtiyar) and are responsible for their decisions. It is like a teacher who knows a student will fail an exam — the teacher’s knowledge did not cause the failure; the student’s lack of revision did.

Sunni view: Al-Qadr is one of the Six Articles of Faith. Sunni Muslims generally emphasise that everything happens according to Allah’s will. Even suffering and hardship are part of His plan. This belief gives comfort in difficult times — if something bad happens, a Muslim can trust it is part of Allah’s greater purpose, even if they cannot understand it.

Shi’a view: Shi’a Muslims place greater emphasis on Adalat (divine justice). They argue that Allah’s justice means He would not predetermine someone to sin and then punish them for it — that would be unjust. Shi’a theology therefore gives more weight to human free will, arguing that people genuinely choose their actions and are justly accountable for them.

Belief in Al-Qadr influences Muslims in practical ways. It encourages Sabr (patience) during hardship, because Muslims trust that suffering is part of Allah’s plan. It also encourages gratitude in good times, since all blessings come from Allah. However, it does not encourage passivity — Muslims are still expected to work hard, make good choices and strive to follow Allah’s guidance.

The Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din)

Muslims believe that this life is a test, and that every person will face judgement before Allah at the end of time. The Day of Judgement is described vividly in the Qur’an as a terrifying, earth-shaking event. Surah 99:1–2 states: “When the earth is shaken with its earthquake, and the earth discharges its burdens.”

On this day, the angel Israfil will blow a trumpet, and all living things will die. Then a second blast will resurrect every person who has ever lived. Each person will stand before Allah and their book of deeds — recorded by the angels throughout their life — will be opened. Those who receive their book in the right hand will enter paradise; those who receive it in the left hand will face punishment.

Surah 99:7–8 states: “Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it. And whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.” This teaches that no action — however small — escapes Allah’s notice. Every good deed and every sin will be accounted for.

Surah 23:102–103 describes the scales of judgement: “Those whose scales are heavy [with good deeds] will be the successful ones. But those whose scales are light will have lost their souls; in hell they will abide.” Good deeds are weighed against bad deeds, and the balance determines a person’s fate.

Akhirah — Life After Death

Akhirah means life after death. Muslims believe the afterlife is eternal and that this earthly life is merely a temporary test. What a person does in this life determines their fate in the next. This belief underpins Muslim morality — every action carries consequences that extend beyond death.

Jannah (Paradise): The Qur’an describes Jannah as a place of eternal peace, pleasure and closeness to Allah. Surah 47:15 describes rivers of water, milk, wine and honey, with fruits of every kind and forgiveness from Allah. Jannah has multiple levels, with the highest reserved for the most righteous. It is the ultimate reward for those who lived according to Allah’s will.

Jahannam (Hell): Jahannam is a place of torment and punishment for those who rejected Allah or lived sinfully without repentance. The Qur’an describes fire, boiling water and suffering. Surah 4:56 describes how the skin of those in hell will be replaced so they continue to feel the punishment. Most Muslims believe Jahannam can be temporary for sinful Muslims — Allah may forgive them and eventually admit them to paradise — but it is eternal for those who committed Shirk (associating partners with Allah).

Key Fact

Belief in Akhirah means Muslims see this life as a preparation for eternity. Every deed is recorded and will be judged. This motivates Muslims to pray, give charity, avoid sin and follow the Qur’an and Sunnah — because the stakes are not just for this life but for the life to come.

Human Responsibility and Accountability

The concepts of predestination, judgement and the afterlife work together to create a strong framework of personal accountability. Muslims believe every person is responsible for their own actions. No one can carry another’s sins (Surah 17:15). On the Day of Judgement, there are no excuses — the angels’ records are complete and Allah’s judgement is perfect.

This accountability influences how Muslims live. It encourages honesty, generosity, compassion and obedience to Allah. It discourages dishonesty, cruelty and arrogance, because Muslims know that even the smallest action — an “atom’s weight” — will be seen and judged. The belief in resurrection means there is no escape from this accountability, even in death.

Muslims believe that after death, the soul enters Barzakh — a state of waiting between death and the Day of Judgement. In the grave, two angels (Munkar and Nakir) question the deceased about their faith: “Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your prophet?” A righteous person will answer correctly and experience comfort; a sinful person will struggle and experience suffering. This period lasts until the Day of Resurrection.
