Surah 23:102–103 describes the scales of judgement: “Those whose scales are heavy [with good deeds] will be the successful ones. But those whose scales are light will have lost their souls; in hell they will abide.” Good deeds are weighed against bad deeds, and the balance determines a person’s fate.

Akhirah — Life After Death

Akhirah means life after death. Muslims believe the afterlife is eternal and that this earthly life is merely a temporary test. What a person does in this life determines their fate in the next. This belief underpins Muslim morality — every action carries consequences that extend beyond death.

Jannah (Paradise): The Qur’an describes Jannah as a place of eternal peace, pleasure and closeness to Allah. Surah 47:15 describes rivers of water, milk, wine and honey, with fruits of every kind and forgiveness from Allah. Jannah has multiple levels, with the highest reserved for the most righteous. It is the ultimate reward for those who lived according to Allah’s will.

Jahannam (Hell): Jahannam is a place of torment and punishment for those who rejected Allah or lived sinfully without repentance. The Qur’an describes fire, boiling water and suffering. Surah 4:56 describes how the skin of those in hell will be replaced so they continue to feel the punishment. Most Muslims believe Jahannam can be temporary for sinful Muslims — Allah may forgive them and eventually admit them to paradise — but it is eternal for those who committed Shirk (associating partners with Allah).

Key Fact

Belief in Akhirah means Muslims see this life as a preparation for eternity. Every deed is recorded and will be judged. This motivates Muslims to pray, give charity, avoid sin and follow the Qur’an and Sunnah — because the stakes are not just for this life but for the life to come.

Human Responsibility and Accountability

The concepts of predestination, judgement and the afterlife work together to create a strong framework of personal accountability. Muslims believe every person is responsible for their own actions. No one can carry another’s sins (Surah 17:15). On the Day of Judgement, there are no excuses — the angels’ records are complete and Allah’s judgement is perfect.

This accountability influences how Muslims live. It encourages honesty, generosity, compassion and obedience to Allah. It discourages dishonesty, cruelty and arrogance, because Muslims know that even the smallest action — an “atom’s weight” — will be seen and judged. The belief in resurrection means there is no escape from this accountability, even in death.

Muslims believe that after death, the soul enters Barzakh — a state of waiting between death and the Day of Judgement. In the grave, two angels (Munkar and Nakir) question the deceased about their faith: “Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your prophet?” A righteous person will answer correctly and experience comfort; a sinful person will struggle and experience suffering. This period lasts until the Day of Resurrection.

title: Jihad
content_html:
Jihad — Striving in the Way of God

The word jihad is one of the most misunderstood terms in Islam. It simply means “struggle” or “striving” and refers to the effort every Muslim must make to follow God’s path. Islam distinguishes between two forms of jihad: greater jihad and lesser jihad.

Greater Jihad — The Inner Struggle

Greater jihad is the daily personal battle every Muslim faces to live according to Allah’s will. It includes resisting temptation, overcoming selfishness, being honest, showing compassion, and striving to become a better person. The Prophet Muhammad is reported to have told soldiers returning from battle: “You have come from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the struggle of a person against their own desires” (Hadith).

Key Fact

Greater jihad is considered more important than lesser jihad because it is a lifelong, continuous struggle. It includes studying the Qur’an, performing the Five Pillars, treating others justly, resisting greed and selfishness, and striving to improve oneself spiritually. Every Muslim engages in greater jihad every day.

Lesser Jihad — The Physical Struggle

Lesser jihad refers to the physical or military struggle to defend Islam when it is under threat. It is permitted only as a last resort and is subject to strict conditions. The Qur’an states: “Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits” (Qur’an 2:190). This verse makes clear that aggression and excess are forbidden.

Islamic teaching sets strict conditions that must be met before lesser jihad can be declared:

It must be defensive: Lesser jihad is only permitted to protect Islam, Muslim lands or oppressed people from attack. Aggressive warfare for conquest, territory or personal gain is forbidden.

It must be a last resort: All peaceful means of resolving the conflict — negotiation, diplomacy, treaties — must be exhausted first.

It must be declared by a recognised religious authority: No individual or group can declare jihad on their own. It requires the authority of a legitimate Muslim leader or scholar.

It must be proportionate: The Qur’an forbids excess (“do not overstep the limits” — 2:190). Civilians, women, children, the elderly, crops and livestock must not be targeted. Prisoners must be treated humanely.

It must stop when the enemy seeks peace: “If they incline towards peace, you must incline towards it too” (Qur’an 8:61).

Key Fact

Lesser jihad is only permitted when it is defensive, a last resort, declared by a legitimate authority, proportionate, and must cease when the enemy seeks peace. The Qur’an explicitly forbids aggression: “Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits” (2:190).

Both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims recognise greater and lesser jihad. However, jihad holds a particularly prominent place in Shi’a Islam as one of the Ten Obligatory Acts. Some Shi’a scholars have historically taught that only a divinely appointed Imam has the authority to declare lesser jihad, which in practice means it cannot be declared while the twelfth Imam remains in occultation. This view restricts the circumstances under which lesser jihad can occur. Other Shi’a scholars argue that senior religious leaders may authorise defensive action in the Imam’s absence.

Islamic Festivals and Commemorations

Festivals play an important role in Muslim life, bringing communities together in celebration and remembrance. The specification requires knowledge of three: Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Fitr, and Ashura.

Id-ul-Adha — The Festival of Sacrifice

Id-ul-Adha falls during the month of Dhul Hijjah and coincides with the Hajj pilgrimage. It commemorates the moment when Ibrahim was willing to sacrifice his son in obedience to God’s command. At the last moment, God provided a ram to sacrifice instead, showing that Ibrahim had passed the ultimate test of faith. Muslims around the world — not just those on Hajj — celebrate by sacrificing an animal (usually a sheep, goat or cow). The meat is divided into three portions: one for the family, one for friends and neighbours, and one for the poor.

Id-ul-Fitr — The Festival of Breaking the Fast

Id-ul-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. After a month of fasting, prayer and self-reflection, Muslims celebrate with special prayers at the mosque, new clothes, festive meals, gifts and visiting family and friends. Before the Eid prayer, Muslims pay Zakat-ul-Fitr — a small charitable donation to ensure that even the poorest members of the community can join in the celebration. It is a day of gratitude to Allah for the strength to complete the fast and a time of joy shared with the whole community.

Ashura falls on the 10th day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar. Its meaning differs greatly between Sunni and Shi’a Muslims.

For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is a day of voluntary fasting. It commemorates the day when God saved the Prophet Musa (Moses) and the Israelites from the Pharaoh by parting the Red Sea. Muhammad fasted on this day and encouraged his followers to do the same.

For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year. It commemorates the martyrdom of Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, who was killed at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Husayn had refused to pledge allegiance to the Umayyad Caliph Yazid, whom Shi’a Muslims considered unjust and illegitimate. His death is seen as the ultimate sacrifice for justice and truth. Shi’a Muslims observe Ashura with mourning processions, dramatic re-enactments of the Battle of Karbala, and expressions of grief. It is a day of deep sorrow, not celebration.

Key Fact

Ashura shows the sharpest divide between Sunni and Shi’a practice. Sunni Muslims observe it as a day of fasting linked to Musa (Moses). Shi’a Muslims observe it as a day of intense mourning for Husayn’s martyrdom at Karbala in 680 CE — one of the most significant events in Shi’a history.

title: Tawhid, the Nature of Allah & Angels
content_html:
Tawhid — The Oneness of God

Tawhid is the single most important belief in Islam. It means the absolute oneness of Allah — there is no God but Allah, and nothing can be compared to Him. Tawhid is the foundation of everything a Muslim believes and does. It is the first part of the Shahadah (declaration of faith): “There is no God but Allah.”

Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) is the key Qur’anic text on Tawhid. It declares: “He is Allah, the One. Allah is Eternal and Absolute. None is born of Him, He is unborn. There is none like unto Him.” This short surah makes clear that Allah is unique, has always existed, was never created and cannot be compared to anything in creation.

Key Fact

Surah 112:1–4 is essential for the exam. It states that Allah is One, Eternal and Absolute, was not born and did not give birth, and nothing is comparable to Him. This surah is recited daily by Muslims and summarises the entire concept of Tawhid.

The opposite of Tawhid is Shirk — associating partners with Allah or giving God-like qualities to anything else. Shirk is considered the worst sin in Islam and the only sin Allah will not forgive. This is why Muslims do not create images of Allah or Muhammad, and why Islamic art uses geometric patterns and calligraphy rather than depictions of God.

The Nature and Qualities of Allah

Muslims believe Allah has many qualities, described throughout the Qur’an. You need to know five key attributes:

Omnipotence (Al-Qadir): Allah is all-powerful. He created the universe from nothing and sustains all life. Nothing is beyond His ability. Surah 2:20 states: “Allah has power over everything.”

Beneficence (Ar-Rahman): Allah is all-good and provides for His creation. Every surah of the Qur’an except one opens with: “In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.” Allah provides food, water, shelter and guidance for all people.

Mercy (Ar-Rahim): Allah is the Most Merciful. He forgives those who sincerely repent. Surah 39:53 says: “Do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.” Muslims believe Allah’s mercy outweighs His wrath.

Fairness and Justice (Al-Adl): Allah treats all people fairly and never acts unjustly. Every person will be judged equally on the Day of Judgement. This quality is especially emphasised in Shi’a Islam as Adalat, one of the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din.

Justice (Adalat in Shi’a Islam): While both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims agree that Allah is just, Shi’a Islam elevates this quality to one of its core beliefs. Surah 16:90 states: “Indeed Allah commands you towards justice.” This means Allah will hold everyone accountable and will never punish the innocent.

Immanence and Transcendence

The spec asks about two contrasting ideas regarding Allah’s relationship with the world:

Transcendence means Allah is beyond and above creation. He exists outside of time, space and the physical world. Muslims emphasise that Allah is utterly different from anything humans can imagine — this is why Surah 112 says “There is none like unto Him.” Allah cannot be fully understood by the human mind.

Immanence means Allah is present and involved in the world. Despite being beyond creation, Allah is closer to every person than their own jugular vein (Surah 50:16). He hears prayers, guides individuals and intervenes in the world. Muslims experience Allah’s immanence through prayer, the Qur’an and the natural world.

Key Fact

Muslims believe Allah is both transcendent (above and beyond creation) and immanent (close and involved in the world). These ideas are not contradictory — Allah is so powerful that He can be beyond the universe and yet closer to a person than their own jugular vein (Surah 50:16).

Angels (Malaikah)

Belief in angels is the second article of Sunni faith. Malaikah are beings created by Allah from divine light (Nur). Unlike humans, angels have no free will — they obey Allah’s commands without question. Surah 35:1 describes them as “messengers with two, three, four pairs of wings.”

Jibril (Gabriel) is the most important angel. He delivered the Qur’an to the Prophet Muhammad over a period of 23 years, beginning in 610 CE during the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr). Without Jibril, Muhammad would not have received Allah’s revelation, and the Qur’an would not exist. Jibril also appeared to Ibrahim and Maryam (Mary), making him the chief messenger between Allah and humanity.

Mika’il (Michael) is the angel of mercy and provision. He is responsible for providing nourishment to human bodies and souls, and controls the natural world — rain, weather and harvest. Muslims believe Mika’il distributes Allah’s blessings throughout creation.

Angels perform several roles: they deliver revelations from Allah to prophets, they record every person’s good and bad deeds (the recording angels sit on each shoulder), they welcome the righteous into paradise, and they will be present at the Day of Judgement. The angel Israfil will blow the trumpet to announce the Day of Judgement, and Azra’il (the Angel of Death) takes souls at the moment of death.

Belief in angels influences Muslims today because it reminds them that their actions are always being recorded. This encourages moral behaviour, honesty and mindfulness in daily life. If a Muslim is tempted to do wrong, the knowledge that an angel is recording the deed acts as a powerful deterrent.

Angels are central to Islam because they connect Allah to humanity. Without Jibril, the Qur’an would not have been revealed. Without the recording angels, there would be no account of human deeds for the Day of Judgement. Belief in Malaikah therefore reinforces belief in the Qur’an, prophethood and the afterlife — linking multiple articles of faith together.

title: Hajj
content_html:
Zakah — Almsgiving

Zakah is the third pillar of Islam and means “purification” or “growth.” By giving away a portion of their wealth, Muslims purify what remains and acknowledge that all wealth ultimately belongs to Allah. It is not considered charity in the voluntary sense — it is a compulsory duty for every Muslim whose savings exceed a minimum threshold called the nisab.

Key Fact

Muslims must give 2.5% of their annual savings above the nisab threshold. The Qur’an specifies eight categories of people who may receive Zakah, including the poor, the needy, those in debt, and travellers in difficulty (Qur’an 9:60).

Origins and Purpose

Zakah has its origins in the Qur’an and the practice of the Prophet Muhammad. The Qur’an links prayer and charity repeatedly: “Establish prayer and pay Zakah” (Qur’an 2:43). This shows that worship of God and care for others are inseparable in Islam. The purpose of Zakah is threefold: it purifies the giver from greed and selfishness, it supports those in genuine need, and it reduces inequality within the ummah.

For the giver: Zakah purifies wealth by removing attachment to material possessions. It reminds Muslims that everything they own is a trust from Allah and develops generosity and compassion. Muslims believe that giving Zakah brings spiritual reward and protects them on the Day of Judgement.

For the recipient: Zakah provides essential support for the poor, the sick, travellers in need and those in debt. It helps prevent extreme poverty and ensures basic needs are met. The Qur’an identifies eight specific categories of recipient (9:60), ensuring money reaches those who need it most.

For the community: Zakah reduces the gap between rich and poor, creating a more just and equal society. It strengthens social bonds within the ummah because the wealthy are directly responsible for supporting the vulnerable. In some Muslim-majority countries, Zakah is collected and distributed by the state.

Khums means “one fifth” and is an additional financial duty unique to Shi’a Islam. Shi’a Muslims pay 20% of their surplus income (after living expenses) each year. Half of the Khums goes to Sayyids (descendants of the Prophet) and half to religious scholars and institutions. Khums is one of the Ten Obligatory Acts and reflects the Shi’a emphasis on supporting the Prophet’s family and the religious leadership.

Key Fact

Zakah (2.5% of savings) is paid by all Muslims, while Khums (20% of surplus income) is an additional duty for Shi’a Muslims. Both serve the purpose of social justice and redistributing wealth, but Khums also supports the Prophet’s descendants and Shi’a religious institutions.

Hajj — Pilgrimage to Makkah

Hajj is the fifth pillar of Islam. Every Muslim who is physically and financially able must make the pilgrimage to Makkah at least once in their lifetime. Hajj takes place during the Islamic month of Dhul Hijjah and attracts over two million Muslims from around the world each year. The Qur’an states: “Pilgrimage to the House is a duty owed to God by people who are able to undertake it” (Qur’an 3:97).

Origins

Hajj traces its origins to the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham). Muslims believe that Ibrahim and his son Isma’il built the Ka’aba as the first house of worship dedicated to the one true God. Many of the rituals performed during Hajj commemorate events from Ibrahim’s life — his willingness to sacrifice his son, his wife Hajar’s search for water, and his rejection of Satan’s temptations.

How Hajj is Performed

Hajj lasts five to six days and involves a series of rituals at sacred sites in and around Makkah. Before beginning, pilgrims enter a state of ihram — they wear simple white garments (two unstitched cloths for men), symbolising equality before God. All distinctions of wealth, status and nationality are stripped away.

Tawaf: Pilgrims walk around the Ka’aba seven times in an anti-clockwise direction. This represents the unity of Muslims in worshipping one God. The Ka’aba is believed to be directly below God’s throne in heaven.

Sa’i: Pilgrims walk seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa, re-enacting Hajar’s desperate search for water for her son Isma’il. This commemorates God’s provision of the Zamzam well.

Arafat: Pilgrims travel to the plain of Arafat and stand in prayer and reflection from noon to sunset. This is considered the most important ritual of Hajj — the Prophet Muhammad said: “Hajj is Arafat.” It represents standing before God on the Day of Judgement.

Muzdalifah: After sunset at Arafat, pilgrims travel to Muzdalifah where they pray, rest under the open sky, and collect pebbles for the next day’s ritual.

Mina — Stoning the Pillars: At Mina, pilgrims throw pebbles at three stone pillars representing the places where Ibrahim rejected Satan’s temptations. This symbolises the Muslim’s rejection of evil and temptation in their own life.

Sacrifice: An animal (usually a sheep or goat) is sacrificed at Mina, commemorating Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son in obedience to God. The meat is distributed to the poor. This coincides with the festival of Id-ul-Adha celebrated by Muslims worldwide.

Key Fact

The key stages of Hajj include Tawaf (circling the Ka’aba), Sa’i (walking between Safa and Marwa), standing at Arafat, collecting pebbles at Muzdalifah, stoning the pillars at Mina, and animal sacrifice. Each ritual commemorates events from the life of Ibrahim and symbolises key aspects of Muslim faith.

title: Angels and Predestination
content_html:
Risalah — Prophethood

Risalah means prophethood. Muslims believe Allah did not leave humanity without guidance — He sent prophets (messengers) at different times throughout history to teach people how to live according to His will. Prophets are human beings chosen by Allah. They are not divine, but they are considered sinless (ma’sum) and perfectly obedient to God.

The Qur’an mentions 25 prophets by name, but Muslims believe there were many more — some traditions say 124,000. Every nation received at least one prophet. The specification requires knowledge of three key prophets: Adam, Ibrahim (Abraham) and Muhammad.

Adam was the first human and the first prophet. Allah created Adam from clay and breathed life into him. Adam was placed in the Garden of Eden with Hawwa (Eve). When they disobeyed Allah by eating from the forbidden tree, they were sent to earth. However, Adam repented sincerely and Allah forgave him. In Islam, Adam is not seen as carrying “original sin” — his repentance was accepted, and every person is born sinless.

Ibrahim (Abraham) is one of the most important prophets in Islam, known as “Khalilullah” — the Friend of Allah. Ibrahim demonstrated perfect submission to God. When Allah commanded him to sacrifice his son Isma’il, Ibrahim was willing to obey, proving his total faith. Allah intervened and provided a ram instead. This event is commemorated during the festival of Id-ul-Adha. Ibrahim also rebuilt the Ka’aba in Makkah with Isma’il, establishing the site of Hajj.

Muhammad is the final and most important prophet — the “Seal of the Prophets” (Khatam an-Nabiyyin). Surah 33:40 states: “Muhammad is… the messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets.” This means no more prophets will come after him. Muhammad received the Qur’an from the angel Jibril over 23 years, beginning in 610 CE. His life and teachings (the Hadith) are a model for all Muslims to follow. Muhammad’s example is known as the Sunnah.

Key Fact

Muhammad is called the “Seal of the Prophets” (Surah 33:40), meaning he is the last and final messenger of Allah. No new prophets will come after him. His message — the Qur’an — is considered the complete and final revelation from God.

The Holy Books (Kutub)

Muslims believe Allah revealed His guidance through several holy books, each given to a different prophet. Belief in these books is the third article of Sunni faith (Kutub). However, Muslims believe that all previous scriptures were either lost, altered or corrupted over time. Only the Qur’an remains in its original, unchanged form.

The Qur’an was revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril over 23 years. It contains 114 surahs (chapters) and is considered the literal, unchanged word of Allah in Arabic. It is the supreme authority in Islam — every other source of guidance is secondary to it. Muslims treat the physical Qur’an with great respect: it is kept on the highest shelf, hands are washed before reading it, and nothing is placed on top of it.

The Torah (Tawrat) was revealed to the Prophet Musa (Moses). It contained Allah’s laws and guidance for the Israelites.

The Psalms (Zabur) were revealed to the Prophet Dawud (David). They contained hymns and praises to Allah.

The Gospel (Injil) was revealed to the Prophet Isa (Jesus). It contained guidance and teachings from Allah for the people of that time.

The Scrolls of Abraham (Suhuf Ibrahim) were among the earliest revelations, given to the Prophet Ibrahim. They have been lost entirely.

Key Fact

The Qur’an has supreme authority in Islam because Muslims believe it is the only holy book that has never been changed or corrupted. It is the direct word of Allah, revealed in Arabic through Jibril, and it supersedes all previous scriptures.

The Qur’an: Revelation and Authority

The Qur’an was revealed to Muhammad beginning on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) in approximately 610 CE. Muhammad was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira near Makkah when the angel Jibril appeared and commanded him to “Read!” (Surah 96:1–5). Muhammad could not read, but the words were pressed into his heart. Revelations continued for the next 23 years until Muhammad’s death in 632 CE.

The Qur’an’s authority in Islam is absolute. It is the primary source of Shari’ah (Islamic law) and provides guidance on worship, morality, family life, justice and social conduct. When a question arises, Muslims turn first to the Qur’an, then to the Hadith and Sunnah, and then to scholarly interpretation.

The Imamate in Shi’a Islam

The Imamate is the fourth root of Usul ad-Din and is unique to Shi’a Islam. Shi’a Muslims believe that after Muhammad’s death, leadership of the Muslim community should have passed to his cousin and son-in-law Ali, and then through a line of twelve Imams descended from Muhammad’s family (Ahl al-Bayt).

Divine appointment: Shi’a Muslims believe each Imam was chosen by Allah, not elected by the community. This gives them a religious authority that Sunni caliphs did not claim.

Infallibility: The Imams are considered ma’sum (sinless and infallible). They cannot make mistakes in matters of faith and are perfect interpreters of the Qur’an and Islamic law.

The Twelfth Imam: Shi’a Muslims believe the twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, went into “occultation” (hiding) in 874 CE. He is believed to be alive and will return at the end of time as a messianic figure to establish justice and peace on earth.

Influence today: Because the twelfth Imam is in hiding, Shi’a scholars (ayatollahs and mujtahids) act as his representatives, interpreting Islamic law on his behalf. This gives senior Shi’a clergy a level of religious authority that has no parallel in Sunni Islam.

The Imamate is a key difference between Sunni and Shi’a Islam. Sunni Muslims do not believe in divinely appointed, infallible leaders after Muhammad. They followed elected caliphs and rely on scholarly consensus for interpretation of Islamic law. For Shi’a Muslims, the Imamate is not merely a political institution — it is a core theological belief about how Allah continues to guide humanity.

title: Salah & Sawm
content_html:
Salah — The Second Pillar

Salah is the second of the Five Pillars and the most regular act of worship in a Muslim’s life. It is not simply asking God for things — it is a structured, formal act of submission to Allah that involves the whole body and mind. The Qur’an commands: “Establish prayer for My remembrance” (Qur’an 20:14).

The Five Daily Prayers

Sunni Muslims pray at five set times each day, calculated from the position of the sun. The times shift slightly throughout the year. This constant rhythm of prayer is designed to keep Allah at the centre of a Muslim’s day, no matter what else they are doing.

Key Fact

The five daily prayers are: Fajr (before sunrise), Zuhr (just after midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (just after sunset), and Isha (night). Shi’a Muslims perform the same five prayers but may combine Zuhr with Asr and Maghrib with Isha, praying three times a day.

Preparing for Prayer — Wudu

Before praying, Muslims must perform wudu — a ritual washing that prepares the body and mind for standing in God’s presence. Wudu involves washing the hands, mouth, nose, face, forearms up to the elbows, wiping the head and ears, and washing the feet up to the ankles. The Qur’an instructs: “You who believe, when you are about to pray, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, wash your feet up to the ankles” (Qur’an 5:6). If water is unavailable, Muslims may use clean earth or sand in a practice called tayammum.

Direction, Movements and Recitations

All Muslims face the direction of the Ka’aba in Makkah when they pray. In a mosque, the mihrab shows this direction. Each prayer consists of a set number of rak’ah — cycles of standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, accompanied by recitations from the Qur’an in Arabic. The physical act of prostration — placing the forehead on the ground — symbolises total submission to Allah.

Muslims can pray anywhere that is clean — at home, at work, or outdoors. However, praying in the mosque is considered more meritorious, especially for men. Muhammad said that prayer in congregation is “twenty-seven times more rewarding than prayer performed individually” (Hadith, Sahih al-Bukhari). In the mosque, an imam leads the prayer, and worshippers stand in rows facing the mihrab. Women may pray in a separate area or at home. At home, Muslims use a prayer mat and a compass to find the direction of Makkah.

Jummah is the Friday congregational prayer, held at the mosque just after midday. It replaces the normal Zuhr prayer. All adult male Muslims are expected to attend, and women may also attend. The imam delivers a khutbah (sermon) covering religious guidance, moral teaching and community matters. The Qur’an instructs: “Believers! When the call to prayer is made on the day of congregation, hurry towards the reminder of God and leave off your trading” (Qur’an 62:9). Jummah strengthens the ummah by bringing Muslims together as a community each week.

Key Fact

Sunni and Shi’a Muslims both perform the five daily prayers, but Shi’a Muslims often combine them into three sessions. Shi’a Muslims may also place a small clay tablet called a turbah on the ground to prostrate upon, as they believe the forehead should touch natural earth rather than carpet.

Sawm — Fasting During Ramadan

Sawm is the fourth pillar of Islam. During the holy month of Ramadan, Muslims fast from dawn (Fajr) to sunset (Maghrib). They abstain from all food, drink, smoking and sexual relations during daylight hours. The fast is broken each evening with a meal called iftar, often shared with family and community.

Origins and Significance

Ramadan is the month in which the Qur’an was first revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril. The Qur’an commands: “It was in the month of Ramadan that the Qur’an was revealed as guidance for mankind. So any one of you who is present that month should fast” (Qur’an 2:185). Fasting teaches self-discipline, empathy for the poor, and gratitude to Allah for His provision.

Benefits of fasting: Sawm develops taqwa (God-consciousness), strengthens willpower, creates empathy with those who go hungry, and brings the community together through shared iftar meals and increased mosque attendance. Muslims believe fasting purifies the soul and brings them closer to Allah.

Exceptions: Certain people are exempt from fasting: young children, the elderly, pregnant or breastfeeding women, people who are ill, travellers, and those menstruating. Most of these people are expected to make up the missed days later or feed a poor person for each day missed.

Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power): This falls within the last ten nights of Ramadan and commemorates the night the Qur’an was first revealed. The Qur’an says: “The Night of Power is better than a thousand months” (Qur’an 97:3). Many Muslims spend the entire night in prayer, believing that worship on this night earns greater reward than a thousand months of ordinary worship.

Key Fact

Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power) falls in the last ten nights of Ramadan. It commemorates the first revelation of the Qur’an and is described as “better than a thousand months” (Qur’an 97:3). Many Muslims spend the night in prayer and reflection.

title: Jihad & Islamic Festivals
content_html:
Jihad — Striving in the Way of God

The word jihad is one of the most misunderstood terms in Islam. It simply means “struggle” or “striving” and refers to the effort every Muslim must make to follow God’s path. Islam distinguishes between two forms of jihad: greater jihad and lesser jihad.

Greater Jihad — The Inner Struggle

Greater jihad is the daily personal battle every Muslim faces to live according to Allah’s will. It includes resisting temptation, overcoming selfishness, being honest, showing compassion, and striving to become a better person. The Prophet Muhammad is reported to have told soldiers returning from battle: “You have come from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the struggle of a person against their own desires” (Hadith).

Key Fact

Greater jihad is considered more important than lesser jihad because it is a lifelong, continuous struggle. It includes studying the Qur’an, performing the Five Pillars, treating others justly, resisting greed and selfishness, and striving to improve oneself spiritually. Every Muslim engages in greater jihad every day.

Lesser Jihad — The Physical Struggle

Lesser jihad refers to the physical or military struggle to defend Islam when it is under threat. It is permitted only as a last resort and is subject to strict conditions. The Qur’an states: “Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits” (Qur’an 2:190). This verse makes clear that aggression and excess are forbidden.

Islamic teaching sets strict conditions that must be met before lesser jihad can be declared:

It must be defensive: Lesser jihad is only permitted to protect Islam, Muslim lands or oppressed people from attack. Aggressive warfare for conquest, territory or personal gain is forbidden.

It must be a last resort: All peaceful means of resolving the conflict — negotiation, diplomacy, treaties — must be exhausted first.

It must be declared by a recognised religious authority: No individual or group can declare jihad on their own. It requires the authority of a legitimate Muslim leader or scholar.

It must be proportionate: The Qur’an forbids excess (“do not overstep the limits” — 2:190). Civilians, women, children, the elderly, crops and livestock must not be targeted. Prisoners must be treated humanely.

It must stop when the enemy seeks peace: “If they incline towards peace, you must incline towards it too” (Qur’an 8:61).

Key Fact

Lesser jihad is only permitted when it is defensive, a last resort, declared by a legitimate authority, proportionate, and must cease when the enemy seeks peace. The Qur’an explicitly forbids aggression: “Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits” (2:190).

Both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims recognise greater and lesser jihad. However, jihad holds a particularly prominent place in Shi’a Islam as one of the Ten Obligatory Acts. Some Shi’a scholars have historically taught that only a divinely appointed Imam has the authority to declare lesser jihad, which in practice means it cannot be declared while the twelfth Imam remains in occultation. This view restricts the circumstances under which lesser jihad can occur. Other Shi’a scholars argue that senior religious leaders may authorise defensive action in the Imam’s absence.

Islamic Festivals and Commemorations

Festivals play an important role in Muslim life, bringing communities together in celebration and remembrance. The specification requires knowledge of three: Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Fitr, and Ashura.

Id-ul-Adha — The Festival of Sacrifice

Id-ul-Adha falls during the month of Dhul Hijjah and coincides with the Hajj pilgrimage. It commemorates the moment when Ibrahim was willing to sacrifice his son in obedience to God’s command. At the last moment, God provided a ram to sacrifice instead, showing that Ibrahim had passed the ultimate test of faith. Muslims around the world — not just those on Hajj — celebrate by sacrificing an animal (usually a sheep, goat or cow). The meat is divided into three portions: one for the family, one for friends and neighbours, and one for the poor.

Id-ul-Fitr — The Festival of Breaking the Fast

Id-ul-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. After a month of fasting, prayer and self-reflection, Muslims celebrate with special prayers at the mosque, new clothes, festive meals, gifts and visiting family and friends. Before the Eid prayer, Muslims pay Zakat-ul-Fitr — a small charitable donation to ensure that even the poorest members of the community can join in the celebration. It is a day of gratitude to Allah for the strength to complete the fast and a time of joy shared with the whole community.

Ashura falls on the 10th day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar. Its meaning differs greatly between Sunni and Shi’a Muslims.

For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is a day of voluntary fasting. It commemorates the day when God saved the Prophet Musa (Moses) and the Israelites from the Pharaoh by parting the Red Sea. Muhammad fasted on this day and encouraged his followers to do the same.

For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year. It commemorates the martyrdom of Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, who was killed at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Husayn had refused to pledge allegiance to the Umayyad Caliph Yazid, whom Shi’a Muslims considered unjust and illegitimate. His death is seen as the ultimate sacrifice for justice and truth. Shi’a Muslims observe Ashura with mourning processions, dramatic re-enactments of the Battle of Karbala, and expressions of grief. It is a day of deep sorrow, not celebration.

Key Fact

Ashura shows the sharpest divide between Sunni and Shi’a practice. Sunni Muslims observe it as a day of fasting linked to Musa (Moses). Shi’a Muslims observe it as a day of intense mourning for Husayn’s martyrdom at Karbala in 680 CE — one of the most significant events in Shi’a history.

title: Tawhid and the Nature of Allah
content_html:
Tawhid — The Oneness of God

Tawhid is the single most important belief in Islam. It means the absolute oneness of Allah — there is no God but Allah, and nothing can be compared to Him. Tawhid is the foundation of everything a Muslim believes and does. It is the first part of the Shahadah (declaration of faith): “There is no God but Allah.”

Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) is the key Qur’anic text on Tawhid. It declares: “He is Allah, the One. Allah is Eternal and Absolute. None is born of Him, He is unborn. There is none like unto Him.” This short surah makes clear that Allah is unique, has always existed, was never created and cannot be compared to anything in creation.

Key Fact

Surah 112:1–4 is essential for the exam. It states that Allah is One, Eternal and Absolute, was not born and did not give birth, and nothing is comparable to Him. This surah is recited daily by Muslims and summarises the entire concept of Tawhid.

The opposite of Tawhid is Shirk — associating partners with Allah or giving God-like qualities to anything else. Shirk is considered the worst sin in Islam and the only sin Allah will not forgive. This is why Muslims do not create images of Allah or Muhammad, and why Islamic art uses geometric patterns and calligraphy rather than depictions of God.

The Nature and Qualities of Allah

Muslims believe Allah has many qualities, described throughout the Qur’an. You need to know five key attributes:

Omnipotence (Al-Qadir): Allah is all-powerful. He created the universe from nothing and sustains all life. Nothing is beyond His ability. Surah 2:20 states: “Allah has power over everything.”

Beneficence (Ar-Rahman): Allah is all-good and provides for His creation. Every surah of the Qur’an except one opens with: “In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.” Allah provides food, water, shelter and guidance for all people.

Mercy (Ar-Rahim): Allah is the Most Merciful. He forgives those who sincerely repent. Surah 39:53 says: “Do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.” Muslims believe Allah’s mercy outweighs His wrath.

Fairness and Justice (Al-Adl): Allah treats all people fairly and never acts unjustly. Every person will be judged equally on the Day of Judgement. This quality is especially emphasised in Shi’a Islam as Adalat, one of the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din.

Justice (Adalat in Shi’a Islam): While both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims agree that Allah is just, Shi’a Islam elevates this quality to one of its core beliefs. Surah 16:90 states: “Indeed Allah commands you towards justice.” This means Allah will hold everyone accountable and will never punish the innocent.

Immanence and Transcendence

The spec asks about two contrasting ideas regarding Allah’s relationship with the world:

Transcendence means Allah is beyond and above creation. He exists outside of time, space and the physical world. Muslims emphasise that Allah is utterly different from anything humans can imagine — this is why Surah 112 says “There is none like unto Him.” Allah cannot be fully understood by the human mind.

Immanence means Allah is present and involved in the world. Despite being beyond creation, Allah is closer to every person than their own jugular vein (Surah 50:16). He hears prayers, guides individuals and intervenes in the world. Muslims experience Allah’s immanence through prayer, the Qur’an and the natural world.

Key Fact

Muslims believe Allah is both transcendent (above and beyond creation) and immanent (close and involved in the world). These ideas are not contradictory — Allah is so powerful that He can be beyond the universe and yet closer to a person than their own jugular vein (Surah 50:16).

Angels (Malaikah)

Belief in angels is the second article of Sunni faith. Malaikah are beings created by Allah from divine light (Nur). Unlike humans, angels have no free will — they obey Allah’s commands without question. Surah 35:1 describes them as “messengers with two, three, four pairs of wings.”

Jibril (Gabriel) is the most important angel. He delivered the Qur’an to the Prophet Muhammad over a period of 23 years, beginning in 610 CE during the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr). Without Jibril, Muhammad would not have received Allah’s revelation, and the Qur’an would not exist. Jibril also appeared to Ibrahim and Maryam (Mary), making him the chief messenger between Allah and humanity.

Mika’il (Michael) is the angel of mercy and provision. He is responsible for providing nourishment to human bodies and souls, and controls the natural world — rain, weather and harvest. Muslims believe Mika’il distributes Allah’s blessings throughout creation.

Angels perform several roles: they deliver revelations from Allah to prophets, they record every person’s good and bad deeds (the recording angels sit on each shoulder), they welcome the righteous into paradise, and they will be present at the Day of Judgement. The angel Israfil will blow the trumpet to announce the Day of Judgement, and Azra’il (the Angel of Death) takes souls at the moment of death.

Belief in angels influences Muslims today because it reminds them that their actions are always being recorded. This encourages moral behaviour, honesty and mindfulness in daily life. If a Muslim is tempted to do wrong, the knowledge that an angel is recording the deed acts as a powerful deterrent.

Angels are central to Islam because they connect Allah to humanity. Without Jibril, the Qur’an would not have been revealed. Without the recording angels, there would be no account of human deeds for the Day of Judgement. Belief in Malaikah therefore reinforces belief in the Qur’an, prophethood and the afterlife — linking multiple articles of faith together.

title: The Five Pillars, Ten Obligatory Acts & Shahadah
content_html:
The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam

Islam is built on five core duties known as the Five Pillars. Just as the pillars of a building hold up its roof, these five duties hold up the entire faith. If a Muslim neglects any one of them, their spiritual life is weakened. The Prophet Muhammad said: “Islam is built upon five things” (Hadith, Sahih al-Bukhari).

Key Fact

The Five Pillars are: Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (prayer five times daily), Zakah (charitable giving of 2.5% of savings), Sawm (fasting during Ramadan), and Hajj (pilgrimage to Makkah at least once in a lifetime).

The Five Pillars are not optional — they are fard (compulsory) for every adult Muslim of sound mind. They give Muslims a shared identity across the world, uniting the global ummah through common acts of worship, charity and devotion. Whether a Muslim lives in London, Jakarta or Cairo, these duties connect them to every other believer.

Each pillar addresses a different aspect of devotion. The Shahadah establishes belief, Salah maintains daily contact with God, Zakah ensures social responsibility, Sawm builds spiritual discipline, and Hajj connects Muslims to the origins of their faith. Together they form a complete framework for living according to Allah’s will. Neglecting any pillar is considered sinful because each one supports the others.

The Ten Obligatory Acts in Shi’a Islam

Shi’a Muslims — particularly Twelver Shi’a — follow the Ten Obligatory Acts. These include all of the Five Pillars (Salah, Sawm, Zakah, Hajj and Jihad) plus five additional duties that reflect Shi’a theological priorities.

The ten duties are: Salah (prayer), Sawm (fasting), Zakah (almsgiving), Hajj (pilgrimage), Khums (a 20% tax on surplus income), Jihad (striving in the way of God), Amr bil ma’ruf (commanding what is good), Nahi anil munkar (forbidding what is evil), Tawalla (loving the Ahl al-Bayt — the Prophet’s family), and Tabarra (dissociating from the enemies of the Ahl al-Bayt).

The additional duties reflect Shi’a emphasis on social justice, the authority of the Prophet’s family, and the responsibility of every Muslim to actively promote good and resist evil in society. Khums is particularly important because the money is partly given to the descendants of Muhammad, supporting the religious scholars who guide the Shi’a community.

Key Fact

Both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims share the core duties of prayer, fasting, charity and pilgrimage. The key difference is that Shi’a Muslims have additional obligations including Khums (20% tax) and duties related to social justice and loyalty to the Prophet’s family.

The Shahadah — Declaration of Faith

The Shahadah is the first and most fundamental of the Five Pillars. It is a single sentence that captures the entire foundation of Muslim belief:

Key Fact

“La ilaha illa Allah wa-Muhammad rasul Allah” — “There is no God but Allah and Muhammad is the Prophet of Allah.”

The first half of the Shahadah affirms Tawhid — the oneness of God. This rejects any form of Shirk (associating anything with God). The second half acknowledges Muhammad as God’s final messenger, meaning Muslims accept the authority of his teachings and the Qur’an.

The Shahadah in Daily Life

The Shahadah is woven into every stage of a Muslim’s life. It is whispered into the ear of a newborn baby so it is the first thing the child hears. It is recited during every set of daily prayers. Muslims hope it will be the last words they speak before death. Sincerely reciting the Shahadah before Muslim witnesses is the only requirement for converting to Islam — once spoken with genuine belief, a person becomes part of the ummah.

Shi’a Muslims add a third clause to the Shahadah: “and Ali is the friend of God.” This reflects their belief that Ali, the Prophet’s cousin and son-in-law, was divinely appointed as Muhammad’s successor. By including Ali in the declaration of faith, Shi’a Muslims affirm the authority of the Imamate — the line of twelve Imams descended from Ali who they believe are the rightful leaders of Islam.

Why is the Shahadah the Most Important Pillar?

The Shahadah is placed first among the Five Pillars because it is the foundation for everything else. Without sincere belief in one God and the prophethood of Muhammad, the other pillars — prayer, charity, fasting and pilgrimage — would have no meaning. The Qur’an declares: “Your God is one God. There is no deity except Him, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful” (Qur’an 2:163). Every act of Islamic worship flows from this declaration.

Tawhid is not just a belief — it shapes every aspect of a Muslim’s life. If Allah is the only God, then only He deserves worship, obedience and devotion. This means Muslims should not place anything — money, status, other people — above God. Surah 112 states: “He is Allah, the One, Allah is Eternal and Absolute. None is born of Him, He is unborn. There is none like unto Him.” The Shahadah is how Muslims publicly commit themselves to this belief every single day.

title: Akhirah: Life After Death
content_html:
Why Do Muslims Believe in Life After Death?

For Muslims, death is not the end. It marks the beginning of a new stage of existence called Akhirah. This belief shapes how Muslims live every day, because they understand that their actions on Earth will be judged by Allah.

Muslims believe in Akhirah for several important reasons. The Qur’an teaches it directly, and since Muslims believe the Qur’an is the word of Allah, its teachings must be true. The Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) also taught about life after death. Akhirah is one of the Six Articles of Faith in Sunni Islam and connects to Al-Ma’ad (resurrection), one of the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din in Shi’a Islam. Muslims also believe that life is a test from Allah, so there must be a time of reward and punishment to give that test meaning.

Key Fact

Belief in Akhirah is one of the Six Articles of Faith for Sunni Muslims and connects to Al-Ma’ad (resurrection) in the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din for Shi’a Muslims. Both branches agree that all people will face judgement after death.

Barzakh — The Waiting Stage

When a Muslim dies, they enter a stage called Barzakh. This Arabic word means “barrier” — once a person crosses into Barzakh, they cannot return to earthly life. The soul remains conscious in the grave during this period.

Muslims believe that Allah sends two angels to question the dead person about their faith. Those who answer correctly will experience comfort and peace while they wait. Those who deny Allah will face punishment in the grave. The person remains in Barzakh until the Day of Judgement arrives.

Throughout a Muslim’s life, two angels sit on their shoulders recording every action. Raqib sits on the right shoulder and records good deeds, while Atid sits on the left and records bad deeds. These records form the “book of deeds” that will be presented on the Day of Judgement. As the Qur’an states: “The record of their deeds will be laid open and you will see the guilty, dismayed at what they contain” (Qur’an 18:49).

The Day of Judgement

Muslims believe that a day will come when Allah’s purpose for the universe has been fulfilled. The angel Israfil will blow a trumpet to announce the end of the world. The present world will be destroyed and then transformed into a new world. A second trumpet blast will signal the resurrection — every person who has ever lived will be raised from the dead with a new body to stand before Allah.

Allah will then judge each person based on their book of deeds. The Qur’an teaches that if a person receives their book in their right hand, they will enter paradise. If they receive it in their left hand, they will be sent to hell. This judgement is considered fair because Allah gave humans free will, making them responsible and accountable for their choices.

Key Fact

The Shi’a believe in Yawm al-Qiyyamah (the Day of Judgement) as part of Al-Ma’ad. They teach that every Muslim and non-Muslim will be physically resurrected, judged by Allah, and asked to account for every word and action of their lives on Earth.

Jannah — Paradise

Jannah is described in the Qur’an as a beautiful, eternal garden — the final home for the faithful and righteous. The Qur’an promises: “And those who believe and do good deeds, they are dwellers of Paradise, they dwell therein forever” (Qur’an 2:82).

According to Islamic teaching, Jannah has seven levels. Those with the greatest reward will reach the highest levels. People will be asked to recite from the Qur’an, and the more they can recite, the higher they go. In Jannah, families are reunited, no one grows old or becomes ill, and every wish is fulfilled. There are rivers, gardens, beautiful weather, and abundant food.

Muslims believe they will arrive at Jannah over the As-Sirat Bridge. The Qur’an describes Allah saying: “Enter among my servants! Enter My Paradise” (Qur’an 89:29–30). There are believed to be eight gates, each representing a good action such as giving to charity or completing Hajj. A person will be called to the gate that matches their greatest good deed. Two angels welcome people, saying “Peace be upon you — enter here and live within.”

Jahannam — Hell

Jahannam is described as a place of fire and terrible torment. The Qur’an warns: “They will dwell amid scorching wind and scalding water in the shadow of black smoke, neither cool nor refreshing” (Qur’an 56:42–44). It is the punishment for those who reject Allah and commit evil.

There are seven levels of Jahannam, with different punishments for different sins. The most serious sin is shirk (worshipping anything other than Allah), which is the only sin Allah will not forgive. However, for sinful believers, Jahannam can serve as a place of purification. When Allah chooses, He may move these believers on to Jannah.

The Qur’an and Hadith give several reasons why a person may be sent to Jahannam. These include living a wicked life full of evil, rejecting the teachings of the Qur’an, refusing to take responsibility for one’s sins by blaming others, and committing shirk. Some Muslims believe that polytheists will go to hell permanently, but that some non-Muslim monotheists may still be able to enter Jannah.

How Belief in Akhirah Influences Muslim Life

Belief in the afterlife has a powerful effect on how Muslims live. Because life on Earth is seen as a test from Allah, Muslims strive to do well in order to be rewarded in Akhirah. This belief encourages them to think carefully about their actions, behaviour, and choices every single day.

Key Fact

Belief in Akhirah encourages human responsibility and accountability. It urges Muslims to avoid sin, seek forgiveness when they do wrong, perform sacred duties such as reading the Qur’an and following Shari’ah law, and treat every action as an act of worship (ibadah) to Allah.

Muslims are aware that angels are constantly watching and recording their deeds. This makes them more God-conscious (taqwa) in their daily lives. Belief in Akhirah also gives Muslims a sense of justice — the good will be rewarded and the wicked will be punished — and provides purpose and meaning to their lives on Earth.

title: Zakah and Sawm
content_html:
Salah — The Second Pillar

Salah is the second of the Five Pillars and the most regular act of worship in a Muslim’s life. It is not simply asking God for things — it is a structured, formal act of submission to Allah that involves the whole body and mind. The Qur’an commands: “Establish prayer for My remembrance” (Qur’an 20:14).

The Five Daily Prayers

Sunni Muslims pray at five set times each day, calculated from the position of the sun. The times shift slightly throughout the year. This constant rhythm of prayer is designed to keep Allah at the centre of a Muslim’s day, no matter what else they are doing.

Key Fact

The five daily prayers are: Fajr (before sunrise), Zuhr (just after midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (just after sunset), and Isha (night). Shi’a Muslims perform the same five prayers but may combine Zuhr with Asr and Maghrib with Isha, praying three times a day.

Preparing for Prayer — Wudu

Before praying, Muslims must perform wudu — a ritual washing that prepares the body and mind for standing in God’s presence. Wudu involves washing the hands, mouth, nose, face, forearms up to the elbows, wiping the head and ears, and washing the feet up to the ankles. The Qur’an instructs: “You who believe, when you are about to pray, wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows, wipe your heads, wash your feet up to the ankles” (Qur’an 5:6). If water is unavailable, Muslims may use clean earth or sand in a practice called tayammum.

Direction, Movements and Recitations

All Muslims face the direction of the Ka’aba in Makkah when they pray. In a mosque, the mihrab shows this direction. Each prayer consists of a set number of rak’ah — cycles of standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, accompanied by recitations from the Qur’an in Arabic. The physical act of prostration — placing the forehead on the ground — symbolises total submission to Allah.

Muslims can pray anywhere that is clean — at home, at work, or outdoors. However, praying in the mosque is considered more meritorious, especially for men. Muhammad said that prayer in congregation is “twenty-seven times more rewarding than prayer performed individually” (Hadith, Sahih al-Bukhari). In the mosque, an imam leads the prayer, and worshippers stand in rows facing the mihrab. Women may pray in a separate area or at home. At home, Muslims use a prayer mat and a compass to find the direction of Makkah.

Jummah is the Friday congregational prayer, held at the mosque just after midday. It replaces the normal Zuhr prayer. All adult male Muslims are expected to attend, and women may also attend. The imam delivers a khutbah (sermon) covering religious guidance, moral teaching and community matters. The Qur’an instructs: “Believers! When the call to prayer is made on the day of congregation, hurry towards the reminder of God and leave off your trading” (Qur’an 62:9). Jummah strengthens the ummah by bringing Muslims together as a community each week.

Key Fact

Sunni and Shi’a Muslims both perform the five daily prayers, but Shi’a Muslims often combine them into three sessions. Shi’a Muslims may also place a small clay tablet called a turbah on the ground to prostrate upon, as they believe the forehead should touch natural earth rather than carpet.

Sawm — Fasting During Ramadan

Sawm is the fourth pillar of Islam. During the holy month of Ramadan, Muslims fast from dawn (Fajr) to sunset (Maghrib). They abstain from all food, drink, smoking and sexual relations during daylight hours. The fast is broken each evening with a meal called iftar, often shared with family and community.

Origins and Significance

Ramadan is the month in which the Qur’an was first revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril. The Qur’an commands: “It was in the month of Ramadan that the Qur’an was revealed as guidance for mankind. So any one of you who is present that month should fast” (Qur’an 2:185). Fasting teaches self-discipline, empathy for the poor, and gratitude to Allah for His provision.

Benefits of fasting: Sawm develops taqwa (God-consciousness), strengthens willpower, creates empathy with those who go hungry, and brings the community together through shared iftar meals and increased mosque attendance. Muslims believe fasting purifies the soul and brings them closer to Allah.

Exceptions: Certain people are exempt from fasting: young children, the elderly, pregnant or breastfeeding women, people who are ill, travellers, and those menstruating. Most of these people are expected to make up the missed days later or feed a poor person for each day missed.

Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power): This falls within the last ten nights of Ramadan and commemorates the night the Qur’an was first revealed. The Qur’an says: “The Night of Power is better than a thousand months” (Qur’an 97:3). Many Muslims spend the entire night in prayer, believing that worship on this night earns greater reward than a thousand months of ordinary worship.

Key Fact

Laylat al-Qadr (the Night of Power) falls in the last ten nights of Ramadan. It commemorates the first revelation of the Qur’an and is described as “better than a thousand months” (Qur’an 97:3). Many Muslims spend the night in prayer and reflection.

title: Risalah, Holy Books & Prophethood
content_html:
Risalah — Prophethood

Risalah means prophethood. Muslims believe Allah did not leave humanity without guidance — He sent prophets (messengers) at different times throughout history to teach people how to live according to His will. Prophets are human beings chosen by Allah. They are not divine, but they are considered sinless (ma’sum) and perfectly obedient to God.

The Qur’an mentions 25 prophets by name, but Muslims believe there were many more — some traditions say 124,000. Every nation received at least one prophet. The specification requires knowledge of three key prophets: Adam, Ibrahim (Abraham) and Muhammad.

Adam was the first human and the first prophet. Allah created Adam from clay and breathed life into him. Adam was placed in the Garden of Eden with Hawwa (Eve). When they disobeyed Allah by eating from the forbidden tree, they were sent to earth. However, Adam repented sincerely and Allah forgave him. In Islam, Adam is not seen as carrying “original sin” — his repentance was accepted, and every person is born sinless.

Ibrahim (Abraham) is one of the most important prophets in Islam, known as “Khalilullah” — the Friend of Allah. Ibrahim demonstrated perfect submission to God. When Allah commanded him to sacrifice his son Isma’il, Ibrahim was willing to obey, proving his total faith. Allah intervened and provided a ram instead. This event is commemorated during the festival of Id-ul-Adha. Ibrahim also rebuilt the Ka’aba in Makkah with Isma’il, establishing the site of Hajj.

Muhammad is the final and most important prophet — the “Seal of the Prophets” (Khatam an-Nabiyyin). Surah 33:40 states: “Muhammad is… the messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets.” This means no more prophets will come after him. Muhammad received the Qur’an from the angel Jibril over 23 years, beginning in 610 CE. His life and teachings (the Hadith) are a model for all Muslims to follow. Muhammad’s example is known as the Sunnah.

Key Fact

Muhammad is called the “Seal of the Prophets” (Surah 33:40), meaning he is the last and final messenger of Allah. No new prophets will come after him. His message — the Qur’an — is considered the complete and final revelation from God.

The Holy Books (Kutub)

Muslims believe Allah revealed His guidance through several holy books, each given to a different prophet. Belief in these books is the third article of Sunni faith (Kutub). However, Muslims believe that all previous scriptures were either lost, altered or corrupted over time. Only the Qur’an remains in its original, unchanged form.

The Qur’an was revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril over 23 years. It contains 114 surahs (chapters) and is considered the literal, unchanged word of Allah in Arabic. It is the supreme authority in Islam — every other source of guidance is secondary to it. Muslims treat the physical Qur’an with great respect: it is kept on the highest shelf, hands are washed before reading it, and nothing is placed on top of it.

The Torah (Tawrat) was revealed to the Prophet Musa (Moses). It contained Allah’s laws and guidance for the Israelites.

The Psalms (Zabur) were revealed to the Prophet Dawud (David). They contained hymns and praises to Allah.

The Gospel (Injil) was revealed to the Prophet Isa (Jesus). It contained guidance and teachings from Allah for the people of that time.

The Scrolls of Abraham (Suhuf Ibrahim) were among the earliest revelations, given to the Prophet Ibrahim. They have been lost entirely.

Key Fact

The Qur’an has supreme authority in Islam because Muslims believe it is the only holy book that has never been changed or corrupted. It is the direct word of Allah, revealed in Arabic through Jibril, and it supersedes all previous scriptures.

The Qur’an: Revelation and Authority

The Qur’an was revealed to Muhammad beginning on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) in approximately 610 CE. Muhammad was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira near Makkah when the angel Jibril appeared and commanded him to “Read!” (Surah 96:1–5). Muhammad could not read, but the words were pressed into his heart. Revelations continued for the next 23 years until Muhammad’s death in 632 CE.

The Qur’an’s authority in Islam is absolute. It is the primary source of Shari’ah (Islamic law) and provides guidance on worship, morality, family life, justice and social conduct. When a question arises, Muslims turn first to the Qur’an, then to the Hadith and Sunnah, and then to scholarly interpretation.

The Imamate in Shi’a Islam

The Imamate is the fourth root of Usul ad-Din and is unique to Shi’a Islam. Shi’a Muslims believe that after Muhammad’s death, leadership of the Muslim community should have passed to his cousin and son-in-law Ali, and then through a line of twelve Imams descended from Muhammad’s family (Ahl al-Bayt).

Divine appointment: Shi’a Muslims believe each Imam was chosen by Allah, not elected by the community. This gives them a religious authority that Sunni caliphs did not claim.

Infallibility: The Imams are considered ma’sum (sinless and infallible). They cannot make mistakes in matters of faith and are perfect interpreters of the Qur’an and Islamic law.

The Twelfth Imam: Shi’a Muslims believe the twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, went into “occultation” (hiding) in 874 CE. He is believed to be alive and will return at the end of time as a messianic figure to establish justice and peace on earth.

Influence today: Because the twelfth Imam is in hiding, Shi’a scholars (ayatollahs and mujtahids) act as his representatives, interpreting Islamic law on his behalf. This gives senior Shi’a clergy a level of religious authority that has no parallel in Sunni Islam.

The Imamate is a key difference between Sunni and Shi’a Islam. Sunni Muslims do not believe in divinely appointed, infallible leaders after Muhammad. They followed elected caliphs and rely on scholarly consensus for interpretation of Islamic law. For Shi’a Muslims, the Imamate is not merely a political institution — it is a core theological belief about how Allah continues to guide humanity.

title: The Five Pillars, Shahadah and Salah
content_html:
The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam

Islam is built on five core duties known as the Five Pillars. Just as the pillars of a building hold up its roof, these five duties hold up the entire faith. If a Muslim neglects any one of them, their spiritual life is weakened. The Prophet Muhammad said: “Islam is built upon five things” (Hadith, Sahih al-Bukhari).

Key Fact

The Five Pillars are: Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (prayer five times daily), Zakah (charitable giving of 2.5% of savings), Sawm (fasting during Ramadan), and Hajj (pilgrimage to Makkah at least once in a lifetime).

The Five Pillars are not optional — they are fard (compulsory) for every adult Muslim of sound mind. They give Muslims a shared identity across the world, uniting the global ummah through common acts of worship, charity and devotion. Whether a Muslim lives in London, Jakarta or Cairo, these duties connect them to every other believer.

Each pillar addresses a different aspect of devotion. The Shahadah establishes belief, Salah maintains daily contact with God, Zakah ensures social responsibility, Sawm builds spiritual discipline, and Hajj connects Muslims to the origins of their faith. Together they form a complete framework for living according to Allah’s will. Neglecting any pillar is considered sinful because each one supports the others.

The Ten Obligatory Acts in Shi’a Islam

Shi’a Muslims — particularly Twelver Shi’a — follow the Ten Obligatory Acts. These include all of the Five Pillars (Salah, Sawm, Zakah, Hajj and Jihad) plus five additional duties that reflect Shi’a theological priorities.

The ten duties are: Salah (prayer), Sawm (fasting), Zakah (almsgiving), Hajj (pilgrimage), Khums (a 20% tax on surplus income), Jihad (striving in the way of God), Amr bil ma’ruf (commanding what is good), Nahi anil munkar (forbidding what is evil), Tawalla (loving the Ahl al-Bayt — the Prophet’s family), and Tabarra (dissociating from the enemies of the Ahl al-Bayt).

The additional duties reflect Shi’a emphasis on social justice, the authority of the Prophet’s family, and the responsibility of every Muslim to actively promote good and resist evil in society. Khums is particularly important because the money is partly given to the descendants of Muhammad, supporting the religious scholars who guide the Shi’a community.

Key Fact

Both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims share the core duties of prayer, fasting, charity and pilgrimage. The key difference is that Shi’a Muslims have additional obligations including Khums (20% tax) and duties related to social justice and loyalty to the Prophet’s family.

The Shahadah — Declaration of Faith

The Shahadah is the first and most fundamental of the Five Pillars. It is a single sentence that captures the entire foundation of Muslim belief:

Key Fact

“La ilaha illa Allah wa-Muhammad rasul Allah” — “There is no God but Allah and Muhammad is the Prophet of Allah.”

The first half of the Shahadah affirms Tawhid — the oneness of God. This rejects any form of Shirk (associating anything with God). The second half acknowledges Muhammad as God’s final messenger, meaning Muslims accept the authority of his teachings and the Qur’an.

The Shahadah in Daily Life

The Shahadah is woven into every stage of a Muslim’s life. It is whispered into the ear of a newborn baby so it is the first thing the child hears. It is recited during every set of daily prayers. Muslims hope it will be the last words they speak before death. Sincerely reciting the Shahadah before Muslim witnesses is the only requirement for converting to Islam — once spoken with genuine belief, a person becomes part of the ummah.

Shi’a Muslims add a third clause to the Shahadah: “and Ali is the friend of God.” This reflects their belief that Ali, the Prophet’s cousin and son-in-law, was divinely appointed as Muhammad’s successor. By including Ali in the declaration of faith, Shi’a Muslims affirm the authority of the Imamate — the line of twelve Imams descended from Ali who they believe are the rightful leaders of Islam.

Why is the Shahadah the Most Important Pillar?

The Shahadah is placed first among the Five Pillars because it is the foundation for everything else. Without sincere belief in one God and the prophethood of Muhammad, the other pillars — prayer, charity, fasting and pilgrimage — would have no meaning. The Qur’an declares: “Your God is one God. There is no deity except Him, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful” (Qur’an 2:163). Every act of Islamic worship flows from this declaration.

Tawhid is not just a belief — it shapes every aspect of a Muslim’s life. If Allah is the only God, then only He deserves worship, obedience and devotion. This means Muslims should not place anything — money, status, other people — above God. Surah 112 states: “He is Allah, the One, Allah is Eternal and Absolute. None is born of Him, He is unborn. There is none like unto Him.” The Shahadah is how Muslims publicly commit themselves to this belief every single day.
